title: How Autocratic Are You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article gives leaders a concrete diagnostic for a trait most would deny having: autocratic control. Rather than asking leaders to self-assess directly, the author proposes examining how they launch new projects, using a three-tier framework of giving background, offering instruction, and mandating direction. The argument is that the frequency with which a leader defaults to instruction or mandate — rather than background — is a more reliable measure of autocratic tendency than self-perception, since many leaders who see themselves as empowering actually default to control more than they realize. The piece acknowledges autocratic leadership has legitimate uses in emergencies but argues it corrodes morale and retention when overused.
points: The best diagnostic for autocratic tendency isn't self-perception but observing how a leader launches new projects across the background/instruction/mandate spectrum.
Autocratic leadership speeds decisions and suits emergencies, but its default overuse predictably produces low morale and talent attrition.
Leaders who consider themselves inclusive often mandate direction far more than they realize, exposing a gap between self-image and behavior.
quotes: An autocratic leadership style is characterized by a leader who makes decisions unilaterally without input from others, dictates rules, policies, and procedures without discussion, and directs team members on both what to do and how to do it.
But while the controlling nature of an autocratic leader can lead to efficient outcomes, it typically results in low morale, dissatisfaction, and an inability to retain top talent.
We can reliably say that the more often a leader offers guidance through instruction or mandates, the more autocratic they are, irrespective of their self-perception.
In contrast, leaders who mandate direction give others little room to operate creatively.
Not surprisingly, some leaders who believe themselves to be highly inclusive and empowering managers turn to the autocratic style much more often than they should.
